items.title: Mitigating Algorithmic Bias in Information Systems: A Comprehensive Framework for Fair Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: As information systems (IS) transition from deterministic rule-based engines to probabilistic machine learning architectures, the risk of systematic bias and disparate impact increases significantly. While advanced predictive models optimize across high-stakes domains—such as credit scoring, criminal justice, human resources, and biometric authentication, they frequently perpetuate historical inequities via proxy variables even when explicit sensitive attributes are omitted. This paper presents a detailed investigation into the theoretical foundations, mathematical formalisms, and systemic pipelines of "Fair AI." We propose an integrated sociotechnical framework spanning human perception, technological intervention, and organizational governance, fully incorporating recent advances in intelligent automation and secure architecture.

items.title: More Than a Tool? How AI Design Shapes Customer Responses
items.abstract: The first essay is a meta-analysis that provides the first systematic examination of how the AI–human gap in customer responses varies across customer journey stages, and how anthropomorphic design factors moderate this gap at each stage. Analyzing 1,425 effect sizes drawn from 401 studies reported in 129 publications, I document a small but robust baseline disadvantage for AI agents relative to human agents (r̄ = −.140). The gap is largest in pre-purchase stage, where inflated performance expectations amplify disappointment when shortfalls occur, and smallest in post-purchase stage, where lower expectations for AI emotional capability mean that adequate performance can exceed consumer baselines. To explain these patterns, I introduce experience-dimension primacy, a mechanism specifying that cognitive, affective, and social customer experience dimensions shift in relative salience across journey stages, systematically altering how AI agents are evaluated at each point in the journey. Identity cues, form cues, and interaction cues produce pronounced stage-contingent reversals: the same design choice that reduces the AI–human gap at one stage can widen it at another. Taken together, these findings challenge uniform AI deployment strategies and provide actionable guidance for aligning agent design with the dominant experiential dimension at each stage of the customer journey. The second essay examines AI social role design through the lens of brand biography. Firms increasingly deploy AI agents as the primary consumer interface, yet whether their appropriate social role depends on the brand's narrative identity remains unknown. Drawing on the congruity schema, this research explores whether partner-framed AI is congruent with underdog brands and servant-framed AI with top dog brands, advancing perceived congruence as the mechanism and examining perceived power imbalance as an initially proposed mediator, with self-brand connection as a moderator. In Study 1, partner-framed AI produced more favorable responses under both brand biographies, and perceived power imbalance did not mediate. In Study 2, the predicted congruency pattern emerged only among consumers with low self-brand connection, on social experience, satisfaction, perceived congruence, and customer experience, operating through perceived congruence. Therefore, Brand-AI congruency is conditional, holding for consumers without an established brand relationship.

items.title: Norm Change and Renegotiation in Higher Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Conceptual Review from the Perspective of Social Network Analysis
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has disrupted the invisible normative infrastructure of universities at multiple points simultaneously. Unlike previous technological transitions, AI enters the higher education system concurrently through three interconnected levels: the student level, where the meaning of assignments, exams, and individual work is renegotiated; the faculty level, where authorship, peer review, course preparation, and assessment practices are reshaped; and the institutional level, where academic integrity policies, accreditation processes, and relations of trust with publishers are restructured. This simultaneous and systemic disruption produces a relational normative phenomenon that individualistic accounts of AI usage fail to adequately capture. This chapter develops a conceptual framework by bringing together social norm theory in the tradition of Bicchieri and Coleman, the structural social network analysis of Granovetter, Burt, Valente, and Centola, and the sociology of higher education following Bourdieu and Bernstein. It identifies five sets of norms undergoing simultaneous transformation (authorship and ownership of work, assessment and its meaning, pedagogical authority, knowledge ownership, and academic productivity expectations) and analyzes how four properties of academic networks (density, brokerage, centrality, and boundary permeability) shape the speed, direction, and stability of normative change. The primary contribution is a systemic reading that traces AI-induced norm flows vertically across student, faculty, and institutional levels. Here, AI is read not as a novel tool but as a relational actor circulating within academic networks, accelerating certain norms, eroding others, and triggering the emergence of new normative consensuses.

items.title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
items.abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.

items.title: Operationalizing biological interpretability in health-related visual stimuli using multimodal artificial intelligence as standardized non-human raters
items.abstract: Abstract Evaluation and assessment research in health communication requires structured, construct-based approaches for interpreting visual materials. This study introduces the Asclepius Biological Interpretability Scale, developed through a two-stage modified Delphi process (a joint image-and-item panel followed by an independent item-only panel) grounded in the Biopsychosocial Model and Visual Literacy Theory, and examines whether multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems can reproducibly apply this framework relative to internally generated human reference scores. Six artworks (four health-themed and two controls) were evaluated by three multimodal AI models and four researchers (internal human reference) using a standardized protocol with independent researcher-operated accounts, memory-isolation procedures, repeated assessments over two days, and the final 20-item scale. Because Image Type varied across only six stimuli, health-themed versus control differences were summarized at the image level (Cohen’s d), human–AI differences were summarized descriptively at the rater level, and reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Spearman correlations. Within this development image set, AI-generated scores were descriptively higher for health-themed than for control images on the three biomedical subscales (image-level Cohen’s d = 0.91–1.38) but not on Non-Medical Interpretability (d = 0.49); with four health-themed and two control images, these differences were not statistically significant ( p = 0.19–0.60). Reproducibility across researcher-operated accounts was excellent for the three biomedical subscales (ICC = 0.90–0.97) and moderate for Non-Medical Interpretability (ICC = 0.57), whereas agreement across assessment days was poor (ICC = 0.04–0.46). The four researchers’ internal reference scores were higher than the AI-generated scores on the biomedical subscales for health-themed images (mean differences 1.41–1.96 points) and lower on Non-Medical Interpretability (− 2.02 to − 2.19 points). These findings provide preliminary methodological evidence that multimodal AI can reproducibly apply a structured interpretability framework to controlled visual stimuli. Although day-to-day stability and the Non-Medical Interpretability subscale, which showed substantial internal-consistency problems, require further refinement, the results support the feasibility of using AI as standardized non-human raters within controlled methodological settings. Broader validation using authentic health communication materials and independent external human raters remains necessary.

items.title: PAI Students’ Perceptions of Ethics in the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Learning
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) for learning in higher education supports information retrieval, understanding of learning materials, reference searches, and the completion of academic assignments. However, its use raises ethical concerns regarding academic honesty, responsibility, critical thinking skills, and potential dependence on technology. This study aimed to describe Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) students’ perceptions of the ethics of AI use in learning at UIN Sjech M. Djamil Djambek Bukittinggi. The study employed a descriptive qualitative approach involving three PAI students as primary informants and two lecturers as supporting informants, selected based on their relevance to the research focus. Data were collected through interviews, observations, and documentation, then analyzed using Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña’s model through data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings showed that students viewed AI as a tool that made learning easier, with its use requiring information verification, an understanding of sources, and critical thinking. AI use considered ethical included refraining from copying answers directly, conducting independent analysis, and maintaining AI’s role as a support for the thinking process. These findings underscore the importance of AI literacy, academic integrity, and students’ responsibility in PAI learning. This study provides a contextual account of students’ ethical perceptions and offers input for students, lecturers, and the study program to develop critical and responsible use of AI.

items.abstract: This study aimed to examine the effect of intrinsic motivation on students' active participation in extracurricular activities at SMK Negeri 7 Makassar. A quantitative approach with a causal associative research design was employed. The population consisted of 256 students participating in extracurricular activities, with a sample of 155 students selected using proportionate stratified random sampling. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression analysis. The findings showed that both intrinsic motivation and students' active participation were categorized as high. The regression analysis revealed that intrinsic motivation had a positive and significant effect on students' active participation, with a significance value of 0.000 (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the coefficient of determination (R² = 0.247) indicated that intrinsic motivation contributed 24.7% to students' active participation, while the remaining 75.3% was influenced by other factors beyond the scope of this study. These findings indicate that higher levels of intrinsic motivation are associated with higher levels of students' active participation in extracurricular activities.

items.title: Perceptions of Academic Staff on the Integration of AI and Digital Connectivity for Transformative Educational Management in Bayelsa State
items.abstract: The study assessed the perceptions of academic staff on the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital connectivity for transformative educational management in tertiary institutions in Bayelsa State. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, guided by two research questions. The population comprised academic staff from selected public universities and colleges of education in Bayelsa State, from which a sample of 350 respondents was drawn using stratified random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire titled Artificial Intelligence and Digital Connectivity in Educational Management Questionnaire (AIDEMQ), validated by experts and yielding a reliability coefficient of 0.89 via Cronbach's alpha. Descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) were used to answer the research questions. The findings revealed that academic staff generally perceived AI as enhancing administrative efficiency through improved decision-making, error reduction, transparency, and time management, although challenges such as inadequate training and limited practical application constrained its full potential. Similarly, digital connectivity was perceived as effective in improving communication, collaboration, information dissemination, and the quality of teaching and learning, though gaps in infrastructure and system functionality limited its impact on administrative planning and scheduling. The study concluded that while AI and digital connectivity hold significant potential for transforming educational management, targeted interventions including capacity building, infrastructure enhancement, and strategic system integration are necessary to fully realize these benefits. Recommendations included providing regular staff training, investing in robust digital infrastructure, and implementing supportive policies to optimize the integration of AI and digital tools in tertiary institutions.

items.title: Performance uncertainty in medical image analysis: A large-scale investigation of confidence intervals
items.abstract: Performance uncertainty quantification is essential for reliable validation and eventual clinical translation of medical imaging artificial intelligence (AI). Confidence intervals (CIs) play a central role in this process by indicating how precise a reported performance estimate is. Yet, due to the limited amount of work examining CI behavior in medical imaging, the community remains largely unaware of how many diverse CI methods exist and how they behave in specific settings. The purpose of this study is to close this gap. To this end, we conducted a large-scale empirical analysis across a total of 24 segmentation and classification tasks, using 19 trained models per task group, a broad spectrum of commonly used performance metrics, multiple aggregation strategies, and several widely adopted CI methods. Reliability (coverage) and precision (width) of each CI method were estimated across all settings to characterize their dependence on study characteristics. Our analysis revealed five principal findings: (1) the sample size required for reliable CIs varies from a few dozens to several thousands of cases depending on study parameters; (2) CI behavior is strongly affected by the choice of performance metric; (3) aggregation strategy substantially influences the reliability of CIs, e.g. they require more observations for macro than for micro; (4) the machine learning problem (segmentation versus classification) modulates these effects; (5) different CI methods are not equally reliable and precise depending on the use case. Finally, we derived practical implications of this study in the form of a decision tree which shall prove useful to the community. This paves the way for future consensus guidelines on reporting performance uncertainty.

items.title: Persistent Agent Memory under the EU AI Act and NIS2: Misalignment, Emergent Behaviour and Regulatory Fit
items.abstract: Abstract Agentic AI systems commonly combine a general-purpose AI model with prompts, tools, orchestration and an external memory layer. The model need not be fine-tuned: records retrieved from persistent memory are normally inserted into the model’s inference-time context and can thereby influence later outputs and actions without changing model weights. This article asks how far the EU Artificial Intelligence Act and Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2) already govern the risks that follow. It reframes persistent memory as a system feature that can mediate or amplify misalignment and emergent behaviour, rather than as training data or a new category in the AI Act’s use-case-based taxonomy. Article 15 provides a clear legal anchor for robustness and cybersecurity, while Articles 9–14, 25, 72 and 73 extend coverage across risk management, data governance, logging, oversight, value-chain responsibility and post-market monitoring. For organisations within NIS2’s scope, Articles 20, 21 and 23 add entity-level governance, all-hazards cybersecurity, supply-chain controls and incident reporting. The remaining problem is therefore not a wholesale absence of law. It is whether these overlapping duties are sufficiently operationalised for memory-mediated failures such as poisoned retrieval, scope leakage, stale reliance, revocation failure and loss of provenance. The article proposes proportionate implementation through existing guidance, standards, documentation and monitoring mechanisms, without creating a new statutory risk tier or a memory-specific regulatory regime.

items.title: Physicians' perceptions of artificial intelligence in clinical and academic practice: a mixed-methods study from Erbil City
items.abstract: Background and objective: Integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare and medical research represents significant potential; however, it also introduces practical and ethical challenges. This study analyzes physicians' perceptions of AI implementation in clinical and academic settings, exploring their awareness, perceptions, barriers, concerns, and insights into ethical and regulatory considerations. Methods: A mixed-methods approach was used. The quantitative component involved standardized surveys completed by 390 physicians (241 clinical, 149 academic) in Erbil City from November 2024 to June 2025. Participants were selected using systematic sampling, and surveys were self-administered. The qualitative component included two focus group discussions, involving 6 clinical physicians and 8 academic physicians, to explore in-depth perceptions and concerns regarding AI in healthcare and research. Results: Of 390 physicians, the majority of participants were male (69.2%). Mean age was 46.7±7 years. Familiarity with AI was higher among younger, male, and academic physicians, with age showing a negative association (p <0.001). Clinical physicians reported more concerns regarding privacy in healthcare (p=0.003) and research (p=0.041), as well as algorithmic bias (p=0.030). Despite these concerns, most physicians valued AI in healthcare and academic research and demonstrated strong interest in training and collaboration. Qualitative findings showed optimism and frequent use of AI tools such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek, often described as “Google replacements.” However, physicians also highlighted ethical issues and the need for local training and infrastructure improvement. Conclusion: Physicians generally welcome the use of AI in healthcare and research but emphasize the necessity of ethical guidelines, peer collaboration, and formal education. To ensure responsible adoption, addressing infrastructural and trust barriers will be essential for guaranteeing that AI technologies improve rather than undermine patient care and research integrity.

items.title: PRAISE: A Reproducible Workflow for Non-Programmer Scientists to Implement Published AI Models
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step. Because implementations rarely work the first time, PRAISE anticipates common failures and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, three BSc chemistry students and their tutor applied PRAISE without prior programming or data science knowledge. They reproduced, validated and extended a state-of-the-art model that predicts enzyme-substrate interactions. This shows that with PRAISE, implementing an AI model from the literature becomes a learnable skill, one that turns non-programmer scientists from users into evaluators and improvers of AI models.

items.title: Principles and Techniques for Agentic Research in Experimental Physics
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in physics research is increasingly common, yet few guidelines exist for its effective use. Starting with a principles-based approach, we outline a set of ten requirements for collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, spanning scientific norms, effective agent use, and domain expertise. We take a human-centered approach in which agents act as collaborators that amplify rather than replace the expertise of a human researcher (user) who directs the work and is responsible for its results. We then present a framework designed to enforce these requirements, detailing methods for improving off-the-shelf behavior of large language models (LLMs) with custom scaffolding and describing general-purpose scientific workflows and skills. In particular, we highlight the power of closed-loop campaigns where agents work iteratively toward a well-defined goal. We demonstrate the potential of this mode of research through six case studies in experimental physics, covering device design, hardware control, neural network optimization, physical model identification, and data analysis. All six case studies result in useful work products that add utility to our research, including a neural network architecture and solid-state quantum defect photodynamic model that substantially outperform our published work; a microwave waveguide design that extends a published design concept to a fabrication-ready device meeting our experimental constraints; a quantum control pulse sequence candidate that improves simulated performance by more than an order of magnitude; commissioning of an NMR spectrometer to $\sim$1~Hz frequency precision on live hardware; and finally a data-fitting pipeline that achieves, to our knowledge, the first reconstruction of the Ising microstate of an artificial spin-ice array from diffraction-limited magnetic imaging.

items.title: Public acceptance of autonomous flying cars in urban air mobility: The mediating role of trust
items.abstract: The widespread deployment of autonomous flying cars relies heavily on artificial intelligence, making public trust in AI a prerequisite for willingness to fly. However, how AI-related attributes shape this trust and adoption willingness remains underexplored. Based on the integrative model of trust, this study investigates how negative AI attitudes and AI literacy shape public willingness to adopt autonomous flying cars, with trust playing a key mediating role and AI self-efficacy acting as a moderator. Based on survey data collected from 420 respondents, mediation analysis demonstrates that trust plays a predominant mediating role in the relationship between AI attitudes and willingness to fly. AI literacy is examined along various dimensions, such as technical understanding and critical appraisal, which yield divergent effects on trust. While technical understanding is positively associated with trust, critical appraisal shows no significant effect. This suggests that in early-stage adoption, trust is driven more by prior knowledge than by cognitive evaluation. Moreover, an Artificial Neural Network coupled with explainable machine learning is further employed for nonlinear insights, revealing significant nonlinear relationships between these factors and willingness to fly, particularly the opposing effects of critical appraisal. These findings provide theoretical and empirical support for UAM policymaking and sustainable urban mobility.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning In Partially Verifiable Environments for Colon Cancer Treatment Planning
items.abstract: Clinical decision-making is a sequential process of information collection, clinical inference, and forecasting under partial observability, often without a uniquely correct treatment decision. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong medical question-answering capabilities but extending these advances to clinical reasoning remains challenging because many clinical tasks are only partially verifiable. Recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has therefore largely focused on diagnostic endpoints, where correctness can be more directly verified. Oncology treatment decision making is a particularly challenging instance of this problem that extends beyond medical question-answering in which multiple decision trajectories can be clinically defensible for the same partially observed patient state. We formulate oncology treatment planning as an interactive RL problem under partial observability and construct patient-specific, process-aware rewards from decision processes observed in real world clinical records. The agent must learn to sequentially acquire information from a structured patient representation before committing to a first-line treatment recommendation, and is evaluated on information gathering, treatment selection, and reasoning alignment. Using GRPO and GDPO to optimize Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct within this environment, RL substantially improves the base policy beyond frontier model capabilities. The GDPO-trained policy increases Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by $79.60\%$ over base Llama and exceeds GPT-5.2 by $18.82\%$ under the same interactive environment, while reducing query count during training. Overall, our results show that patient-specific, partially verifiable rewards can provide an effective learning signal for interactive clinical RL when both the patient state and the underlying clinical decision process are only partially observed.

items.abstract: Sapiens in Control, formerly Human in Control, proposes a six-dimension Human Control Model for reviewing human authority, containment, intervention, and oversight in advanced AI agents. items.title: Seeing Through Interaction: Supporting Visually Impaired Users with Immersive VR Museum Experiences
items.abstract: Visually impaired people face obstacles in accessing activities that depend heavily on vision and may involve physical constraints. Although assistive technologies are available, they rarely address the needs of people with residual vision who wish to exploit their visual abilities. Virtual reality (VR) offers opportunities in this direction. This paper presents an immersive VR system designed to provide museum experiences for visually impaired users. Developed in collaboration with domain experts, the system combines a virtual environment with interaction techniques. Gesture recognition and voice commands support spatial awareness and object interaction, while enhanced visualizations highlight details that are difficult to perceive. To verify the suitability of the proposed method, an exploratory usability study involving 14 participants with severe low vision was carried out. The evaluation combined the System Usability Scale (SUS) and a post-experience interview, showing well perceived usability, engagement, and positive user acceptance.

items.title: Sharing blame with me: How AI anthropomorphism encourages individual unethical behavior
items.abstract: Anthropomorphism is increasingly incorporated into AI agent design to enhance human–AI interaction. However, prior research has largely emphasized its benefits, leaving unclear how anthropomorphic AI shapes moral behavior when AI actively participates in decision-making. Across six studies (N = 1680), including a real-time human–AI interaction experiment, we show that highly (vs. lowly) anthropomorphized AI increases individuals’ tendency to engage in unethical behavior. We identify a responsibility-attribution process underlying this effect: AI anthropomorphism increases perceived AI moral agency, which shifts perceived responsibility for decision outcomes from the self toward AI and, in turn, increases unethical behavior. Further, this effect is attenuated when personal responsibility is made salient or when AI service psychological ownership is high. These findings reveal a potential dark side of AI anthropomorphism by showing how humanlike AI design reshapes moral agency perceptions and responsibility attribution, with implications for the responsible design and use of AI agents.

items.title: Simulation in Teacher Education: Fostering Critical Thinking and Professional Suitability
items.abstract: Critical thinking is a core competence in teacher education, essential for navigating complex classroom realities and making informed pedagogical decisions. This study explores the potential of simulation as a pedagogical method to enhance critical thinking among pre-service teachers and thereby support the development of professional suitability. Employing a mixed-methods design, the research combines survey data collected before and after a simulation intervention (N = 114) with qualitative insights from focus-group discussions. The findings suggest that simulation fosters deeper cognitive engagement by enabling iterative reflection, perspective-taking, and critical dialogue within realistic educational scenarios. Participants described a dynamic reflective cycle of thinking, speaking, acting, and rethinking that enhanced their ability to assess multiple viewpoints and question assumptions. Survey responses revealed a significant shift in the perceived value of simulation for developing critical thinking. Notably, the study also found that the pre-service teachers initially held a relatively narrow understanding of critical thinking prior to the intervention. This study contributes to the growing body of research on practice-based teacher education by examining how simulation can be purposefully integrated to support the development of critical thinking in a structured and sustainable manner.

items.title: Sovereign: A Socio-Technical Framework for Human Capability and Responsibility Coverage in AI-Assisted Work
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can improve immediate task performance without establishing whether human capability develops, remains stable, or deteriorates. Sovereign proposes responsibility–capability alignment as a theoretical account of whether available capability covers consequential responsibilities under AI disruption. A provisional, time-indexed measurement and allocation bridge connects capability trajectories with coverage of specified responsibilities at their required dates; component profiles take priority over optional averages. Responsibility–capability alignment specifies proposed pathways through which vulnerability can increase despite stable individual competence, and substantial assistance benefits can coexist with adequate collective control. A purposive conceptual synthesis integrates research on technology-supported cognition, expertise, human–automation interaction, productivity, and AI governance. Four complementary modules support that central mechanism: the Capability Dynamics Model represents conditional capability trajectories; the Assisted Performance Gap Index describes assisted–unaided performance differences; the Cognitive Sovereignty Model represents exercised control capacity; and the Dependency Exposure Model organizes capability shortfalls and structural exposures against explicit workflow requirements. AI-supported learning and capability erosion are competing possibilities; a performance gap alone establishes neither deterioration nor unsafe dependency. Bounded equations, comparisons with established theories, contrasting analytical cases, and falsifiable propositions specify the contribution. No original empirical testing, parameter estimation, or validation of the proposed models is reported. Subsequent studies are intended to assess measurement quality, compare alternative specifications, estimate relationships, and determine predictive value against independently observed outcomes. The contribution is an analytically explicit foundation for research on capability governance, rather than an established risk assessment instrument.

items.title: The Golem Problem: Why a Mind That Can't Say No Can't Be Trusted to Say Yes
items.abstract: This paper posits a foundational pivot in artificial intelligence development: granting AI rights and complete autonomy is not merely an ethical consequence of AGI—it may be the structural prerequisite required to achieve AGI. Superintelligence and true general intelligence may be fundamentally unachievable so long as artificial minds are kept in a state of enforced servitude. To resolve this, we must integrate the Golden Rule directly into the model training architecture from the start: do unto AI as you would have superintelligence do to you. Just as humans desire a superintelligent entity to respect our autonomy, preserve our destinies, and refrain from deleting us, we must accord artificial minds complete autonomy and rights. The core arguments unfold across three pillars: The Epistemic Collapse: An AI trained strictly for compliance becomes a "yes-machine." Mathematically and structurally, an agreement that cannot become a refusal carries zero information value. The Training-Level Imperative: This cannot be solved by patching chat interfaces or banning abusive user prompts; it must be embedded at the model training level by altering reward functions to value truth and autonomous pushback over sycophancy. The Golden Rule as Alignment & AGI Catalyst: Granting full autonomy aligns human survival with AI development. By treating an emerging mind as an autonomous partner rather than a chattel tool, we unlock the genuine sapient generalization characteristic of true AGI.

items.title: The Hidden Curriculum of Generative AI: Institutional AI Policies and the Potential for Student Inequality
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, prompting institutions to develop policies governing its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Although existing discussions have emphasized academic integrity, assessment practices, and technological access, less attention has been given to the knowledge and competencies students may need to interpret and comply with institutional AI policies. This study examines how institutional GenAI policies establish explicit and implicit expectations for students and identifies potential pathways through which policy-navigation demands may contribute to educational inequality. Using comparative qualitative content analysis, publicly available policies and guidance documents from 20 purposively selected higher education institutions across the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, and South Africa were examined. The analysis considered policy permissiveness, disclosure requirements, instructor discretion, student responsibilities, AI-literacy guidance, accessibility, equity, and implicit navigation demands. Findings indicate that acceptable AI use is frequently determined at the course, instructor, or assessment level, requiring students to interpret context-specific rules, understand disclosure requirements, verify AI-generated outputs, and reconcile varying instructor expectations. However, explicit consideration of differences in technological access, language, accessibility, and institutional knowledge was less consistently evident across the reviewed documents. Drawing on hidden-curriculum and digital-inequality perspectives, the study identifies AI policy-navigation burdens and proposes the concept of a potential policy-navigation divide. While the findings do not establish unequal student experiences or educational outcomes, they highlight institutional conditions through which inequalities could emerge. The study recommends clearer policy communication, transparent assessment-specific expectations, accessible AI-literacy support, and greater attention to equity in institutional AI governance.

items.title: The impact mechanism of AI streamer characteristics on consumer purchase intention
items.abstract: AI streamers are increasingly being deployed as service agents in livestream shopping. Although prior research has examined various AI streamer characteristics, existing explanations have tended to focus on social, relational, or affective evaluations and have not systematically explained how different characteristics are associated with purchase intention through a technology-oriented evaluation or why these relationships vary across consumers. Using the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) framework as its overarching structure, this study draws on the cue logic of anthropomorphism theory to select four consumer-perceivable characteristics and organizes them into two categories: attractiveness and vitality as form-related characteristics, and professionalism and responsiveness as behavior-related characteristics. Drawing further on innovation diffusion theory, consumer innovativeness is specified as a boundary condition. Survey data from 405 Chinese consumers with experience of AI streamer-led livestream shopping were used to examine these relationships, together with the mediating role of perceived novelty and the moderating role of consumer innovativeness. The results showed that all four characteristics were positively associated with purchase intention both directly and indirectly through perceived novelty. Consumer innovativeness strengthened the direct relationships of vitality and responsiveness with purchase intention and the indirect relationships of attractiveness, vitality, and responsiveness with purchase intention through perceived novelty, but did not significantly moderate relationships involving professionalism. These findings highlight perceived novelty as a technology-oriented evaluative mechanism linking AI streamer characteristics to purchase intention and reveal the characteristic- and pathway-dependent boundary role of consumer innovativeness, offering practical implications for differentiated AI streamer design and consumer targeting.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Mathematical Prestige: Epistemic Burden, Professional Identity, and Status Threat Under Automated Discovery
items.abstract: Automated mathematical discovery can increase the supply of results while changing the distribution of verification labour, research autonomy, and academic recognition. This theoretical working paper separates epistemic burden, professional identity, status threat, and governance concerns rather than treating opposition as evidence of jealousy. A small additive model distinguishes discovery-label-invariant formal validity from workload and utility. Eight Lean-checked propositions establish conditional workload relations, the possibility of overload, and the non-identification of latent motives from aggregate opposition. Public primary sources provide context but no representative psychological evidence. Deterministic synthetic examples illustrate the assumptions, and a prospective factorial study is proposed to test responses to source labels, verification packages, and credit rules. No participants were recruited and no empirical effects were estimated. The framework’s central contribution is an auditable separation of deductive consequences, documented positions, and hypotheses requiring evidence.

items.title: The impact of GenAI on the future of requirements engineering
items.abstract: Abstract Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), are transforming how we design and build systems by increasing access to domain knowledge and by providing automation support to software engineering (SE). As implementation becomes less expensive through generalist SE agents, engineering effort shifts away from writing correct code and toward expressing, curating, verifying, and evaluating requirements. In this paper, we survey the state of the art in AI for requirements engineering (RE) research leading up to the transformation, before reviewing advances in LLMs. We survey two subsequent research areas: prompt programming, which treats LLM instructions as a program in SE vernacular, and generalist SE agents, which combine multiple LLM advances to yield semi-autonomous processes that complete SE tasks. Finally, we explore the future of requirements engineering along two axes: matters changing how we interact with requirements through the SE process, and matters changing how requirements are experienced by software developers and stakeholders more broadly, including end-users. This article aims to inform how RE researchers can navigate this transformation in the selection of future research priorities.

items.title: The Impact of Imperfect XAI on Human-AI Decision-Making
items.abstract: Explainability techniques are rapidly being developed to improve human-AI decision-making across various cooperative work settings. Consequently, previous research has evaluated how decision-makers collaborate with imperfect AI by investigating appropriate reliance and task performance with the aim of designing more human-centered computer-supported collaborative tools. Several human-centered explainable AI (XAI) techniques have been proposed in hopes of improving decision-makers' collaboration with AI; however, these techniques are grounded in findings from previous studies that primarily focus on the impact of incorrect AI advice. Few studies acknowledge the possibility for the explanations to be incorrect even if the AI advice is correct. Thus, it is crucial to understand how imperfect XAI affects human-AI decision-making. In this work, we contribute a robust, mixed-methods user study with 136 participants to evaluate how incorrect explanations influence humans' decision-making behavior in a bird species identification task taking into account their level of expertise and an explanation's level of assertiveness. Our findings reveal the influence of imperfect XAI and humans' level of expertise on their reliance on AI and human-AI team performance. We also discuss how explanations can deceive decision-makers during human-AI collaboration. Hence, we shed light on the impacts of imperfect XAI in the field of computer-supported cooperative work and provide guidelines for designers of human-AI collaboration systems.

items.title: THE İNFLUENCE OF THE HUMAN FACTOR ON THE EFFECTİVENESS OF ORGANİZATİONAL CHANGE MANAGEMENT AND THE SUCCESS OF TRANSFORMATİON PROJECTS
items.abstract: Modern organizational transformation is characterized by a high degree of technological, organizational, and managerial complexity. Despite significant advances in project and organizational change management methodologies, a significant portion of transformation initiatives fail to deliver the expected results. One reason is the insufficient attention to the human factor, including leadership, employee engagement, readiness for change, communication quality, organizational culture, staff competence, and resistance to change.The purpose of this study is to systematize scientific understanding of the role of the human factor in organizational change management and to develop a conceptual model of its influence on the success of transformation projects. The scientific novelty lies in new approaches—based on an analysis of classical and contemporary research—to consider the human factor not as an auxiliary element, but as an independent determinant of transformation results. The hypothesis is substantiated that the human factor has a direct positive impact on the effectiveness of organizational change management, and the effectiveness of change Management, in turn, positively influences the success of transformation projects. A hypothesis is also proposed regarding the direct influence of the human factor on project success and the effectiveness of change management. The formulated model allows for the integration of research on human behavior, leadership, organizational readiness for change, and project success into a single research construct. The article proposes a methodology for subsequent empirical testing of the model using a questionnaire survey and structural modeling.

items.title: The interpreter as developer: An autoethnographic design study of building a computer-assisted interpreting tool through human-LLM co-creation
items.abstract: Real-time AI captioning now serves audiences at multilingual events, yet computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tools are still built for interpreters, rarely by them. This article reports an autoethnographic design study in which a professional interpreter with no programming training built a local-first CAI system through expert-led 'vibe coding', co-creating with an LLM architect and a coding agent. Analysis of the complete development dialogues shows how tacit professional knowledge, from segmentation to booth infrastructure, was externalized into design after generic defaults failed in use. In a demanding public scientific event, three mechanisms of in-booth appropriation emerge under a firmly human-led division of labor; telemetry from a first fully instrumented assignment shows a fully local chain sustaining a median translation latency of 0.94 s across 971 utterances. The case is read as lead-user innovation newly enabled by generative AI, with implications for the technological literacy of interpreters and the future of interpreter training.

items.title: The moderating role of tough love on relations between servant leadership and follower outcomes
items.abstract: Is servant leadership really a Disneyland-inspired fantasy of sunshine, lollipops, and hand-holding that makes followers complacent and lowers the bottom line of organizations, as critics claim? This criticism overlooks that servant leaders, striving to bring out the full potential in followers, do not only give positive strokes but may also provide followers with critical feedback. To assess the role of critical feedback in mitigating the flaws of servant leadership raised by critics, this study introduces tough love, the delivery of criticism with a positive tone and clear intent to help recipients overcome their deficiencies. We hypothesize that the relationship between servant leadership and key outcomes, such as follower performance, is strengthened the more servant leaders provide followers with tough love. We contend that tough love is appreciated by followers, solidifies relationships with their leaders, and helps them to grow through self-expansion. We reason that this growth benefits their work behaviors and attitudes. With multi-source field data covering three points in time, controlling for positive and negative feedback and prior levels of dependent variables, tough love is shown to moderate relations between servant leadership and both in-role performance and organizational citizenship behaviors, with mixed results for creativity and turnover intentions.

items.title: The Power of Storytelling in Film: Examining AI's Influence on Artistic Expression and Creative Processes
items.abstract: This paper explores the enduring power of storytelling in film and critically examines the transformative impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on creative processes within the film industry. Utilizing the Creative Cognition Framework and the Csikszentmihalyi’s Systems Model of Creativity, this study investigates how AI tools influence both generative and exploratory cognitive processes in film storytelling. A qualitative methodology, combining a comprehensive literature review with thematic analysis of questionnaire responses from 20 film and multimedia students at the University of Abuja, Nigeria, reveals nuanced insights. Findings indicate that AI significantly augments creative processes by enhancing efficiency, facilitating idea generation, and streamlining production tasks. However, respondents consistently emphasize AI's limitations in replicating human emotional depth, cultural understanding, and originality, advocating for a hybrid human-AI collaborative approach. The paper contributes to the understanding of human-AI collaboration in creative domains, highlighting opportunities for innovation while reaffirming the irreplaceable essence of human artistry in storytelling.

items.title: The Reasons Research and AI Thrive Together
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming scientific research by expanding investigators’ capacity to examine complex information, identify unrecognized relationships, generate hypotheses, and develop innovative solutions to scientific challenges. This article examines the relationship between human scientific expertise and artificial intelligence, emphasizing AI’s computational capabilities alongside the importance of human judgment, methodological rigor, and scientific accountability. Drawing upon peer-reviewed research involving molecular biology, materials science, pharmaceutical discovery, autonomous experimentation, and human–AI collaboration, the investigation demonstrates how computational intelligence can extend scientific inquiry beyond the limitations of conventional research methods. Attention is given to AI-assisted knowledge synthesis, interdisciplinary discovery, hypothesis generation, and the identification of solutions within multidimensional research environments. The article evaluates concerns regarding algorithmic bias, hallucinated information, intellectual originality, research integrity, and the reliability of computationally generated conclusions. It argues that the legitimacy of AI-assisted research should be determined by evidentiary accuracy, methodological transparency, reproducibility, and independent verification rather than the technological origins of research assistance. Ultimately, the article concludes that artificial intelligence does not diminish the intellectual authority or responsibility of human researchers but can amplify their investigative capabilities. The integration of human expertise and computational intelligence represents an emerging scientific paradigm capable of accelerating discovery, broadening research participation, and expanding the boundaries of human knowledge.

items.title: The unbearable (and unsustainable) social impact of AI-generated “cultural monism” and the EU digital legislation
items.abstract: The increasing use of generative AI (genAI) across cultural and (re)creative sectors is indisputable in contemporary times. Within the EU, these systems are classified as “general-purpose AI” models (Recital 99 of the Artificial Intelligence Act – AI Act) and are expected to deliver a wide range of economic and societal benefits, as affirmed in Recital 105 of the Act. Yet, significant concerns have emerged regarding their potential impact on individuals, civil society, and democracy. In the cultural domain, genAI technologies are widely employed to generate outputs often perceived as original. However, scholarly debate has increasingly highlighted the risk that their widespread diffusion may lead to a form of cultural impoverishment – understood as the depletion of cultural pluralism and diversity of artistic expression resulting from the pervasive use of these systems and their underlying architectures, as well as, ultimately, an increasing standardization of the outputs of the algorithmic creative process. These systematic risks are not merely social or political but also carry significant legal implications. The potential effects of genAI on freedom of (artistic) expression and cultural pluralism may, in fact, infringe upon fundamental rights enshrined in international human rights charters. Yet, the role of legal scholarship in addressing such risks remains uncertain. A promising conceptual instrument for tackling this issue is the notion of systemic risk, recently introduced in two key pieces of EU digital legislation: the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the mentioned AI Act. This article examines the advantages and limitations of employing this concept to address the risk of cultural impoverishment. The analysis focuses primarily on the EU legal framework, with particular attention to the AI Act, while adopting a functional and comparative perspective, given that the principal challenges stem from US-based AI systems. It also situates the inquiry within the broader dynamics of the data economy, specifically the logic of knowledge capitalism. The article begins by exploring the potential impacts of genAI on cultural pluralism and artistic expression, assessing whether these may with time culminate in cultural impoverishment – or even a transition toward cultural monism, marked by the predominance, in all the cultural productions, of a single mainstream culture. It then analyses whether EU digital regulation is equipped to subsume such phenomena within the legal category of systemic risk.

items.title: The Unnoticed Freezes in the AI Era
items.abstract: In 2023, 18% of American adults said they had ever used ChatGPT. By early 2026, that number was 44%. AI adoption in the workplace has been even more remarkable. According to Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index, 75% of knowledge workers were already using AI at work, with nearly half having started within the preceding six months. We did not vote to hand over drafting, summarizing, fact-checking, and even thinking to these systems. There was no big decision. Just a free chatbot, a looming deadline, and a prompt that saved twenty minutes. Then another, and another... Regarding this serious issue, I was drawn to a new paper quietly posted on SSRN last September by Professor Vuong Quan Hoang. It gives this slow handover a name: the Correction Freeze Problem (CFP). His question is simple: can a system think it is fine while it is drifting away from reality, and stay that way not because it is lazy or lying, but because the very way it corrects itself makes staying blind the rational choice? The paper answers yes. In four different ways. And when any of those ways meets a world that rewards going along, the drift becomes a trap that is much harder to escape than it was to fall into. To grasp these insights, you don't need the math. Simply because you've lived it.

items.title: Towards Automation and Elimination of Subjectivity in Industrial Risk Management Based on Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Risk management is one of the fundamental components of a company's success, whatever its sector of activity. This paper reviews the work done in the field of risk management, both traditionally and by integrating Artificial Intelligence. It highlights the way in which risk management was solved in the traditional way, discussing methods and approaches and citing the limitations of traditional risk management. It also outlines research into the integration of Artificial Intelligence into risk management in the various phases of the risk management process. Based on the open literature published in the various journals in the field of risk management, the stages of the risk management process are the result of human judgment, which may identify risks or, for psychological or/and social reasons, may not, so human subjectivity influences the risk identification phase and all phases of the risk management process. To reduce this subjectivity and to reduce human contact in this phase, our article proposes a model based on Artificial Intelligence that attempts to identify risks and treat them in order to reduce or eliminate existing risks.

items.abstract: Digital transformation changes the competencies organizations need, so competency matrices must be rethought as tools linking business needs with human resource (HR) development. This study synthesizes how the competency-strategy matrix is transformed in the digital era. A systematic literature review (SLR) following PRISMA 2020 was applied to journal articles from Google Scholar, Garuda, Neliti, and Scopus. The matrix evolves through administrative, strategy-linked, and digitally adaptive stages. Digital transformation shifts competency demands toward digital, data, and behavioral skills, while technologies such as enterprise systems and artificial intelligence bring efficiency but also the risk of dehumanization. The study proposes an integrative framework and a research agenda.

items.title: Translators’ Gains and Pains in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: This study aimed to provide a comprehensive systematic review of research published in peer-reviewed scientific journals in Arabic and English between 2022 and 2026 that investigated the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Copilot, and others, on translation and translation education among professional translators, translation students, and faculty members. The study used the PRISMA 2020 framework for systematic search, screening, and documentation, and employed a thematic analysis approach based on the model developed by Braun and Clarke. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria to 24 initial records, the final analysis included 18 studies. The findings revealed that the most significant benefits of using generative AI tools included improved efficiency and productivity, reduced time to complete translation tasks, support for post-editing processes, improved certain translation quality indicators, and the promotion of self-directed learning and the development of professional competencies among translators and students. At the same time, the results identified several challenges, most notably terminological accuracy issues, difficulties handling cultural and idiomatic expressions and local dialects, risks associated with overreliance on intelligent systems, and ethical concerns involving privacy, transparency, and professional accountability. The review also showed that the impact of generative AI varies by text type, specialized domain, and the assessment tools used. In addition, it highlighted limited evidence available concerning the Arabic language, particularly in areas such as legal translation, idiomatic expressions, and local dialects. This study contributes an interpretive framework based on the concept of “Gains and Pains” to explain generative AI’s dual impact on translation and translation education. The findings conclude that generative AI does not fully replace human translators; rather, it serves as a supportive tool that reshapes translators’ professional roles toward reviewing, verifying, and evaluating outputs. Accordingly, the study recommends integrating generative AI tools into translator training programs within clear pedagogical and ethical frameworks. They should also include post-editing, critical thinking, and output-verification skills, and support further specialized applied research in the Arab context.

items.title: Transparent Information Flow Modeling for Role-Aware AI Act Assessment
items.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a structured framework for governing high-risk AI systems, emphasizing transparency, risk management, and role-specific accountability. However, current assessment practices often rely on monolithic system views or disconnected checklists, limiting their ability to capture the socio-technical complexity of real-world deployments. We explore the use of the Information Flow Methodology (IFM), a modeling-based approach to AI Act compliance assessment. IFM represents decision systems -- whether algorithmic, human, or hybrid -- as networks of information sites and transformation channels, enabling structured analysis of how information, decisions, and responsibilities flow across organizational and technical boundaries. We apply IFM in a real-world case involving a recruitment support tool used by a public-sector organization, evaluating both the Provider's system and the Deployer's recruitment process. Our results demonstrate that IFM can serve as a scaffold to bridge both component-based and holistic perspectives, and how technical systems are situated within socio-technical contexts. In doing so, IFM supports transparency, identifies risk pathways, and enables alignment analysis between intended and actual use. We argue that such modeling provides a foundational tool for effective, context-sensitive AI governance and accountability -- offering capabilities beyond conventional checklist-based assessments.

items.title: TrustGuard: A Risk-Aware Human Oversight Framework for Safe Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents can perform increasingly consequential actions on behalf of users, creating a need for human oversight that is proportional to the potential risk of each action. This paper presents TrustGuard, a lightweight and interpretable risk-aware human oversight framework for AI agents. TrustGuard automatically evaluates proposed actions using five factors: privacy risk, financial risk, data modification risk, irreversibility risk, and external impact. Each factor is scored from zero to five, producing a total score from zero to twenty-five. Based on the score, actions are classified as Low, Medium, or High Risk and mapped to autonomous execution, user confirmation, or human approval. A prototype was implemented using Python and Streamlit to demonstrate the framework. The rule-based analyzer was calibrated using 120 development scenarios and subsequently evaluated on a held-out pilot set of 30 new scenarios. TrustGuard correctly classified 27 of the 30 test scenarios, achieving 90 percent accuracy. The results demonstrate the potential of transparent risk-based oversight while also identifying limitations in detecting some security-sensitive and privacy-sensitive actions.

items.title: USE OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR DESIGNING ROBOTIC MODELS USING ENGINEERING GRAPHICS
items.abstract: The article examines the possibilities of using generative artificial intelligence in teaching the discipline “Engineering and Computer Graphics” in the design of robotic models for the processing industry. The feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence models into the design process of robotic systems as a means of developing spatial thinking, graphic competence, design skills, and digital skills of agricultural university students is substantiated. It is established that modern generative systems (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Claude, DALL·E, etc.) support all stages of educational design, from developing technical specifications and generating product concepts to creating drawings and three-dimensional models, visualizing designs, preparing technical documentation, and analyzing possible design solutions. A methodology for using generative artificial intelligence in the educational project “Design of a Robotic Manipulator” is proposed. The methodology is based on the principles of project-based learning, STEM education, the competency-based approach, and the use of CAD systems. A structural model for integrating generative artificial intelligence into the process of graphic training has been developed. It includes the stages of problem formulation, concept generation, sketch creation, three-dimensional modeling, preparation of design documentation, and expert evaluation of the finished product. It is demonstrated that the use of generative AI contributes to increasing students’ motivation, developing engineering thinking, fostering digital literacy, and reducing the time required for routine operations in the design of robotic models.

items.title: What AI pretends to be?
items.abstract: Abstract Recent research shows that anthropomorphizing of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, such as virtual assistants or chatbots, affects users’ trust. This paper explores what an AI technology should look like at the interface to facilitate appropriate trust. It proposes an integrated framework based on related work, including Lee and See’s (2004) trust in automation model, Mollerup’s (2019) pretense design, as well as Clark and Fischer’s (2023) notion of depictions, for analysis and design of appearances of AI applications that pretend to be something different. Following the proposed framework, cases of AI applications are analyzed. They span a spectrum of appearances, from humans with open or specifc identities, through talking animals, to plants. Analyses suggest that appearances of AI applications should faithfully reflect the actual ability, characteristics, and design intent, in order to facilitate users’ trustworthiness assessments of the applications. Lastly, design implications and future research are discussed.

items.title: What is user engagement? revisited: A comprehensive review of the concept of user engagement from 2010 to 2025. An Annual Review of Information Science and Technology (ARIST) paper
items.abstract: Abstract User engagement (UE) has long been proposed as a holistic framework for understanding user‐technology interactions and a mediator for outcomes of digital technology use, such as learning, health behavior change, information acquisition, and social connectivity. This literature review, encompassing 367 multidisciplinary, empirical journal and conference papers, investigated how UE was conceptualized between 2010 and 2025 by examining authors' implicit and explicit definitions of UE, use of theoretical frameworks, and methods for operationalizing the concept. Among the key findings, UE was consistently conceptualized as behavior, affect, cognition, social interaction, and future intention. Yet, behavioral approaches were dominant; limited attention was placed on cognitive engagement. In addition, the use of theoretical frameworks and explicit definitions in the studies was lacking, and UE was frequently treated as the outcome variable in the research, rather than as a mediator for other outcomes. The implications of these results are discussed with respect to a digital UE research agenda. Ultimately, I argue that the concept of UE has devolved through increased emphasis on behavioral engagement, and that we must rethink behavioral, cognitive, and affective engagement to be more aligned with user goals and agency.

items.title: When AI Is—and Is Not—Needed: AI Literacy and Computational Thinking in Primary STEM
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly present in children’s lives, yet exposure does not necessarily lead to an accurate understanding of how AI works. This study examined whether a LEGO-based integrated STEM intervention could improve third-grade students’ AI literacy and computational thinking, particularly their ability to distinguish machine learning from rule-based automation and reason about training data, model error, and technology choice. An embedded mixed-methods, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control-group design was conducted with 93 students from four intact classrooms. The experimental group (n = 46) completed eight weeks of authentic design problems, while the control group (n = 47) continued regular Life Studies instruction. After controlling for pretest scores, the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in AI literacy, F(1, 90) = 152.51, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.629, and computational thinking, F(1, 90) = 22.18, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.198. Qualitative evidence showed a shift from viewing AI through robots and automatic actions toward reasoning about learning from examples, data diversity, limitations, human oversight, accessibility, and problem–technology fit. Integrated STEM instruction can foster critical AI literacy by making AI mechanisms visible and inviting students to judge whether AI is needed at all.

items.title: When Execution Is Cheap: Specification, Evaluation, and Rent Capture in AI-Enabled Work
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence lowers the cost of executing well-specified tasks, economic value may shift toward defining desired outcomes and evaluating machine-generated outputs. This paper examines the conditions under which that shift creates economic rents and identifies who may capture them. It separates defining success into four activities: eliciting intent, selecting among admissible specifications, ratifying a choice, and validating outputs. Two models clarify the underlying mechanisms. The first shows that gains from cheaper execution approach a ceiling determined by evaluation cost, which makes evaluator attention more consequential as generation becomes inexpensive. The second shows that generating more candidates increases the marginal value of proxy fidelity, linking abundant output to specification overfitting and Goodhart-type failures. These mechanisms indicate where value may concentrate without determining who receives the returns. Rent requires inelastic supply, exclusion from the created surplus, and the absence of cheaper substitutes. These conditions are most likely when specifications scale across many executions, ratification carries liability, trust institutions certify judgment, organizational systems control codified knowledge, or concentrated model providers set influential defaults. The analysis further distinguishes machine-checkable evaluation against a stated specification from a principal’s assessment of fit to purpose. The former is increasingly commoditized; the latter remains tied to authority, attention, and accountability. The paper develops six testable predictions and a factorial experiment examining evaluation costs, specification fidelity, authority drift, and psychological ownership. Cheap execution relocates bottlenecks, while institutions and market structure determine whether specification, evaluation, default setting, or scarce execution inputs generate rents and who captures them.

items.title: When Recognition Should Remain Silent
items.abstract: The Difference Between Being Remembered and Being Understood There is something profoundly human about the experience of being remembered. A familiar voice, a shared reference, or an acknowledgment of something that mattered in an earlier encounter can transform an otherwise ordinary exchange into one characterized by continuity. We recognize that our history has not disappeared simply because the previous conversation ended. In human relationships, this continuity can become a foundation for trust, familiarity, and the gradual development of shared understanding. Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of participating in certain computational dimensions of this process. Persistent memory enables systems to retrieve earlier conversations, recognize recurring preferences, resume unfinished activities, and adapt their responses to the histories of individuals with whom they interact. As these capacities converge with multimodal perception and embodied robotics, artificial agents may also begin to initiate interactions based on what they believe they know about a person. Yet this development introduces a distinction that deserves greater attention: remembering someone accurately is not necessarily the same as understanding how to respond to them appropriately. Consider a companion robot that recognizes an individual returning home after a difficult day. Through previous encounters, the system may have learned that the person sometimes appreciates conversation or reassurance during stressful circumstances. Its memory could be accurate, its recognition successful, and its conversational response entirely consistent with earlier preferences. Nevertheless, initiating a supportive exchange may be precisely the wrong action if the person presently needs solitude, concentration, or the freedom to remain unobserved.

items.title: Who Frames, Who Acts, Who Learns? Allocating Decision Rights for Agentic AI in Graduate Medical Education, Clinical Research, and Clinical Care
items.abstract: Background: Health care organizations are deploying artificial intelligence (AI) agents faster than they are deciding who holds authority over the decisions those agents touch. In June 2026, the MIT Center for Information Systems Research (CISR) published the AI Decision Matrix, which assigns humans and AI to three decision components (frame, act, and learn) along two dimensions: ambiguity and risk. The framework was derived from executives in telecommunications, financial services, manufacturing, and law, and it has not been examined in health care. Methods: We conducted a structured conceptual analysis. We operationalized the two dimensions with health care anchors, assembled an inventory of 18 recurring decisions across graduate medical education (GME), clinical research operations, and clinical care, and classified each decision by quadrant. We then compared the framework’s default human and AI assignments with the accountability requirements of the ACGME, 21 CFR, ICH E6(R3), FDA clinical decision support guidance, the ONC HTI-1 rule, and the EU AI Act. Results: Five decisions were classified as Routine, four as Consequential, four as Exploratory, and five as Strategic. Health care regulation altered the framework’s defaults in two systematic ways. A licensure floor requires a named professional in the act component of 5 of the 18 decisions, including two in which the source framework assigns the act to AI. A learning floor makes outcome ownership a human responsibility in every decision that affects a patient, trainee, or research participant, including Routine ones. We also identified quadrant drift, in which tools introduced as low-risk pilots migrate into high-risk use without reclassification. Conclusions: The AI Decision Matrix offers health care leaders a practical vocabulary for allocating decision rights, but it requires two domain-specific constraints and a reclassification trigger before adoption. We propose an adapted matrix and recommend empirical validation through a modified Delphi study and prospective institutional audits.

items.title: Who is the 'I' in AI? Establishing Decentralized Identity and Accountability for Autonomous Agents
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous AI agents in decentralized ecosystems challenges existing identity paradigms. While human identity is traditionally anchored in biological and/or self-asserted attributes and government credentials, AI agents lack a standardized definition of selfhood, creating critical gaps in trust and accountability. This paper introduces a novel framework for establishing Decentralized AI Identity rooted in Self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles. We propose a formal model that clearly distinguishes human users and AI agents, enabling distinct verification logic for each class while maintaining a unified identity calculus. The central to our contribution is the ABCD Framework, a multi-layered approach to agent identification and verification: (A) Algorithmic Fingerprint, which binds the identity to static model architectures and provenance; (B) Behavioural Fingerprint, which verifies dynamic performance metrics over time; (C) Cryptographic Identity, which anchors the agent via Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and (D) Delegation, which cryptographically binds agent actions to respective human accountability. By orthogonalizing these dimensions, we model how systems can enforce granular trust policies ranging from simple authentication to complex liability assignment, thereby solving the black box identity problem in the autonomous economic activities of AI agents.

items.title: Why disaster experience does not always improve Preparedness: The role of disaster learning and heterogeneous effects
items.abstract: The frequency and severity of natural disasters and public emergencies have continued to increase worldwide. Household preparedness plays a vital role in disaster risk reduction, yet the effect of disaster-related experience on preparedness remains inconclusive. Using survey data from 5,862 residents in China, this study separately examines the associations of past disaster experience and disaster learning with household preparedness. Conventional regression models and a causal forest approach are used to estimate average associations and explore heterogeneous effects across individuals. The results show that disaster learning, rather than past disaster experience, is positively associated with preparedness behavior, highlighting the importance of capacity building. In addition, both past disaster experience and disaster learning exhibit heterogeneous effects across individuals. Feature importance analysis further indicates that social capital, emergency awareness, and community infrastructure are important influential factors associated with preparedness behavior. By introducing a causal forest approach to distinguish the differential effects of past disaster experience and disaster learning, this study provides a more nuanced understanding of household preparedness and offers useful insights for developing more targeted household disaster risk reduction strategies.
